meta.title: Who really said "Death begins in the colon"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Hippocrates. The earliest documented use is a 1944 colon-therapy newspaper ad, and Metchnikoff's 1908 book never uses the phrase.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Death begins in the colon'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Hippocrates. Earliest documented use: a 1944 colon-therapy newspaper advertisement in Oklahoma. Metchnikoff's 1908 book doesn't contain it.

answer.label: Not Hippocrates — an unsourced 20th-century slogan
answer.authorDates: No author identified · earliest documented appearance in print, 24 September 1944
answer.sourceLine: Etymologist Barry Popik’s chronology finds the sentence first in a colon-therapy advertisement in the Daily News-Record of Miami, Oklahoma, dated 24 September 1944 — not in Hippocrates, and not in a text by any of the other men credited with it. Popik notes the line is pinned on both Hippocrates and the Nobel laureate Élie Metchnikoff, but that “it’s not clear what writing of theirs is most similar to the saying.”

source.heading: The earliest documented appearance

docMeta.dd: Dr. J. P. Van Horn — “Colon Therapy—Chiropractic X-ray”
None identified; no Hippocratic text has been pointed to

source.excerpt:
DEATH—
BEGINS IN THE COLON

The pollution of the bloom stream, from poison generated in the lower bowel, does not cause the same kind of malady in all afflicted persons.

(…)

Dr. J. P. VAN HORN
Colon Therapy—Chiropractic X-ray
LADY TECHNICIAN
trail: Barry Popik’s entry, dated 12 September 2011, records that the saying “has been credited to” Hippocrates and to Metchnikoff, “although it’s not clear what writing of theirs is most similar to the saying,” and dates the phrase in print “from at least 1944” — see the citation list ↗.
The same page transcribes a near-variant from The Medical Summary, September 1919: “We don’t know whom to credit for the dictum that ‘Cancer begins in the colon.’” — Popik, 1919 citation ↗.

Metchnikoff’s actual argument is in The Prolongation of Life: the large intestine is “certainly useless in the case of man,” and waste “retained in the large intestine for considerable periods, becomes a nidus for microbes which produce fermentations and putrefaction harmful to the organism.” The phrase itself is absent — search the full text ↗.

Wikiquote’s Hippocrates page carries a Disputed section for exactly this class of line — “Let food be thy medicine and medicine be thy food” is listed there as not found in the Hippocratic corpus — and this quote does not appear on the page at all: Wikiquote: Hippocrates ↗.
source.excerptNote: Transcribed by Barry Popik from Newspapers.com. The reading “bloom stream” is his transcription of the ad as set; “blood stream” is the evident intent. The ellipsis is Popik’s.

source.rightsNote: No author or work of origin has been established, so no rights status can honestly be asserted for the sentence. The earliest documented carrier is an unsigned 1944 American newspaper advertisement; Élie Metchnikoff’s The Prolongation of Life (English translation, 1908) is old enough to be public domain in the United States but does not contain the phrase, so it cannot be the source that clears it.

author.name: Élie Metchnikoff
author.kicker: The science the slogan borrows from
author.heading: Who Élie Metchnikoff actually was
author.metaLine: 1845–1916 · Russian-born biologist at the Pasteur Institute · 1908 Nobel laureate in Physiology or Medicine
author.bio: Metchnikoff shared the 1908 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Paul Ehrlich for work on immunity, then spent his later years at the Pasteur Institute arguing that microbes in the large intestine poison the body and hasten old age — the theory of intestinal auto-intoxication. In The Prolongation of Life: Optimistic Studies he called the human large intestine “certainly useless” and prescribed soured milk to crowd out putrefactive bacteria, which is why he is the figure most often named as the source of this slogan. He never wrote the sentence. The phrase appears nowhere in the 1908 English translation of the book, whose full text is searchable at Project Gutenberg.

misattribution.heading: Four claimants, no text
misattribution.intro: This is a phrase with more credited authors than sources. Each attribution below is real — people really do print it — and each one collapses when you ask for the page it appears on.

items.why: Popular science repeats it as ancient: Ray Kurzweil and Terry Grossman’s Transcend (2011) writes “as Hippocrates observed centuries ago, ‘Death begins in the colon.’” No Hippocratic text has been pointed to. Barry Popik, who compiled the citations, says only that it’s not clear what writing of his is most similar ↗. Hippocrates is a standing magnet for unsourced medical maxims — Wikiquote files “Let food be thy medicine and medicine be thy food” under Disputed ↗, noting it is not found in the Hippocratic corpus.

Bernard Jensen’s Dr. Jensen’s Guide to Diet and Detoxification (2000) opens chapter one by stating the expression “apparently originated with” Metchnikoff during his Pasteur Institute years. The theory did; the sentence did not. A full-text search of the 1908 English translation of The Prolongation of Life ↗ returns no occurrence of “death begins” or “begins in the colon.”

Ted Aloisio’s Blood Never Lies (2004) says the chiropractor Bernard Jensen “coined the phrase” while his medical contemporaries laughed. But the words were already set in a newspaper advertisement in 1944 under a different practitioner’s name, per Popik’s citation list ↗ — and Jensen’s own book credits Metchnikoff, not himself.

Peter Glickman’s Lose Weight, Have More Energy & Be Happier in 10 Days (2005) says the juicing author Norman W. Walker “is credited with the statement.” Credited by whom, and in which of his books, is not said — and the chronology ↗ records no Walker citation.

misattribution.truthLine: No page has ever been produced — not by Hippocrates, Metchnikoff, Jensen or Walker. The earliest appearance Barry Popik records ↗ is a colon-therapy advertisement in the Daily News-Record of Miami, Oklahoma, 24 September 1944, and it spread through naturopathic and chiropractic advertising from 1976 onward.

context.heading: Why a slogan needed a Greek
lead: The idea underneath the phrase is real medical history. Through the nineteenth century, auto-intoxication — the belief that waste held in the bowel poisons the rest of the body — was mainstream doctrine, and Metchnikoff gave it a Nobel laureate’s imprimatur at the Pasteur Institute. What he argued was narrower and stranger than the slogan: that the large intestine is an evolutionary hangover, a reservoir that let running mammals defer defecation, and that the putrefaction it harbours shortens life.

The slogan itself is American, commercial and much later. Popik’s citations are advertisements and lecture write-ups — a chiropractor’s colon-therapy ad in 1944, a Chicago naturopath’s “main tenet” in 1976, ads in California, Georgia and Washington through the 1990s. Attaching it to Hippocrates does a specific job: it converts a sales line into an ancient verdict.
context.detailsSummary: The 1919 near-variant, and what became of the theory
detailsBody: A near-variant ran earlier. In September 1919 The Medical Summary discussed the dictum “Cancer begins in the colon,” adding that “We don’t know whom to credit” for it — the same anonymous-maxim shape, a quarter of a century before the death version surfaces.

By 1997 Edzard Ernst was reviewing auto-intoxication in the Journal of Clinical Gastroenterology and concluding that once “it became clear that the scientific rationale was wrong and colonic irrigation was not merely useless but potentially dangerous, it was exposed as quackery.” The slogan long outlived the doctrine it summarised.
context.pull: “A triumph of ignorance over science” — Edzard Ernst’s 1997 title for the colonic-irrigation revival

sourcesVerified.claim: Barry Popik's entry, dated 12 September 2011, states the saying has been credited to Hippocrates and to Élie Metchnikoff "although it's not clear what writing of theirs is most similar to the saying"; dates "cancer begins in the colon" from at least 1919 and "death begins in the colon" from at least 1944; transcribes the 24 September 1944 Miami (OK) Daily News-Record ad for Dr. J. P. Van Horn; the September 1919 Medical Summary passage; the 1976 Chicago Metro News, 1977 Robesonian, 1979 Merced Sun-Star, 1988 Albany Herald and 1993 Spokesman-Review citations; Bernard Jensen's 2000 chapter crediting Metchnikoff; Ted Aloisio's 2004 claim that Jensen coined it; Peter Glickman's 2005 credit to Norman W. Walker; and Kurzweil & Grossman's Transcend (2011) "as Hippocrates observed centuries ago."

The English translation of Élie Metchnikoff's The Prolongation of Life: Optimistic Studies (edited by P. Chalmers Mitchell, G. P. Putnam's Sons, New York & London, 1908) contains zero occurrences of "death begins" or "begins in the colon"; it does contain "This organ ... is certainly useless in the case of man" and "The accumulation of waste matter, retained in the large intestine for considerable periods, becomes a nidus for microbes which produce fermentations and putrefaction harmful to the organism." Verified by full-text search of the fetched file.

Wikiquote's Hippocrates page has a Disputed section listing "Let food be thy medicine and medicine be thy food" as not found in the Hippocratic corpus, plus "Walking is man's best medicine"; the page does not mention "Death begins in the colon" or "All disease begins in the gut" anywhere.

Wikipedia gives Hippocrates as c. 460 – c. 370 BC, an ancient Greek physician called the Father of Medicine, and states of the Hippocratic Corpus that "The question of whether Hippocrates himself was the author of any of the treatises in the corpus has not been conclusively answered."

Wikipedia gives Élie Metchnikoff as 1845–1916, Russian-born, sharing the 1908 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Paul Ehrlich for work on immunity, appointed at the Pasteur Institute where he remained for the rest of his life, and developing "a theory that aging is caused by toxic bacteria in the gut and that lactic acid could prolong life."

PubMed record 9252839 is E. Ernst, "Colonic irrigation and the theory of autointoxication: a triumph of ignorance over science," J Clin Gastroenterol. 1997 Jun;24(4):196-8, whose abstract states that when "it became clear that the scientific rationale was wrong and colonic irrigation was not merely useless but potentially dangerous, it was exposed as quackery and subsequently went into a decline." Record content confirmed by fetching PMID 9252839 through the NCBI E-utilities efetch endpoint; the pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov HTML page is cookie-walled to automated fetchers.
